newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's NUM to confront JCI on job cuts.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's NUM to confront JCI on job cuts.

text.p: South Africa's National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) said on Friday it would meet JCI Ltd's chairman Mzi Khumalo by Monday to discuss proposed massive job cuts at the newly black-controlled company.
NUM talks with Khumalo are due to follow a mass meeting at the Randfontein Estates Gold Mining Co Ltd on Sunday, where up to 4,100 miners are faced with retrenchment.
"The meeting with Mzi Khumalo will probably be on Sunday evening or at the latest on Monday," NUM general secretary Kgalema Motlanthe told a news conference.
Accusing the industry of shirking its responsibility, Motlanthe said that unless options other than retrenchments were pursued the union might call for a nationwide industry strike.

"We'll leave our options open and if the industry as a whole does not begin to look at other solutions and simply relies on job cutbacks, we have to mobilise for a general strike over this issue in order to save jobs," he said.

JCI workers are not alone in the face of job cuts. Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd's Free State Consolidated Gold Mines Ltd and Vaal Reefs Exploration and Mining Co Ltd have also threatened shaft closures.

Khumalo -- South Africa's first black "randlord" -- took the reins of one of the world's biggest gold mines after his black empowerment consortium African Mining Group bought 34.9 percent of JCI last year.
Motlanthe said he believed JCI had hoped to use Khumalo's appointment to mute the NUM's response to the job cuts.

"They were relying on the fact that...in the euphoria of that sort of change that they could then get away with the job cutbacks. In this present climate of heavy unemployment, they were pushing their luck too far."
JCI announced on Wednesday that it planned to shed between 3,400 and 4,100 Randfontein jobs on May 31 and cut tonnage throughput as part of a far-reaching restructuring programme.

The NUM, saying 3,000 retrechments were also proposed at the Western Areas Gold Mining Co Ltd, announced it would stop Strategic Labour Accord discussions forthwith and withdraw from retrenchment negotiations until a detailed study was held into underlying problems at the two mines.
The union also called on the JCI board to terminate the services of chief executive John Brownrigg for incompetence, blaming him for poor strategic planning.
Motlanthe said the NUM was trying to formulate practical alternatives to job cuts following the posting of poor March quarterly results by the gold mining industry.
Motlanthe also said there was a growing dissatisfaction that the mining industry was exploiting the country's workforce and resources to fund its expansion programmes into Africa.
"Most of the mining groups think that they can simply scale down their operations in South Africa and go to Africa where the mines are not as deep as in this country.
"If anything, this is treacherous," he said, urging the big mining houses to instead look for "greenfields" or new projects inside South Africa which would promote job growth.
Mines statistics show that the number of workers employed on gold mines has fallen sharply to 342,439 by the end of 1996 from 505,262 in 1986.
